items.zh: 持戒清淨 · 明持犯（一）
parent: VI. Distinguishing the Preliminary Expedient Means of Dhyāna-Pāramitā
分別禪波羅蜜前方便第六之一

zh: 第二、明持犯，自有三意：一、略明持犯；二、歷別廣明持犯；三、明覆發。就初總明持犯，有二：一者、持相；二者、犯相。一、持相者，持者，護持。如上所說七種之人受佛禁戒，為十利故，護持無犯。十利者，如毘尼中說：「一、攝僧故；二、極好攝故；三、僧安樂住故；四、折伏高心人故；五、慚愧得安樂住故；六、不信令信故；七、已信增長信故；八、遮今世漏故；九、斷後世惡故；十、令梵行人久住故。」行者一心敬慎，不敢侵毀，如護浮囊，微塵不棄，故名護持，亦名秉持，如持油鉢之喻，是名持相。
en: Second, clarifying upholding and violation: this has three parts in itself — first, briefly clarifying upholding and violation; second, extensively clarifying upholding and violation through each successive stage; third, clarifying concealment and manifestation. As to the first, clarifying upholding and violation as a whole, there are two: first, the mark of upholding; second, the mark of violation.

First, the mark of upholding: "upholding" means guarding and maintaining. As stated above, the seven kinds of persons who receive the Buddha's restraining precepts guard and maintain them without violation for the sake of ten benefits. These ten benefits, as the Vinaya states, are: "First, so as to gather in the saṅgha; second, so as to gather it in most excellently; third, so that the saṅgha may dwell at ease and in joy; fourth, so as to subdue those of arrogant mind; fifth, so that those with a sense of shame may dwell at ease; sixth, so as to bring faith to those without it; seventh, so as to increase the faith of those who already have it; eighth, so as to check the contaminants of the present life; ninth, so as to sever the unwholesome deeds of lives to come; tenth, so that those of pure conduct may long abide." The practitioner, single-mindedly reverent and cautious, dares not encroach upon or damage the precepts — like guarding an inflated float used to cross water, not discarding it even to the smallest degree — hence this is called guarding and maintaining, also called firmly upholding, as in the simile of carrying a bowl brimful of oil. This is the mark of upholding.

zh: 二、明犯相者，犯名違犯。本受佛戒，欲出生死，願求解脫，今遇惡緣，不能自制其心，中途違返，若重若輕，故名違犯。復次，犯名犯觸。猶如服藥，誡忌斷食，不隨醫教，而食惡食，犯觸藥勢，非唯不能愈病，翻致更增，或時至死。犯戒之相亦復如之，故名為犯。
en: Second, clarifying the mark of violation: "violation" means going against and transgressing. One originally receives the Buddha's precepts wishing to leave birth-and-death behind, vowing to seek liberation — but now, encountering an unwholesome condition, being unable to master one's own mind, one turns back midway, whether in a grave or a lesser matter, and this is called going against and transgressing. Furthermore, "violation" also means coming into contact with what harms. It is like someone taking medicine who has been instructed to abstain from certain foods; if they do not follow the physician's instruction and eat something harmful, they come into contact with and undermine the medicine's own power — not only failing to be cured of their illness, but on the contrary making it worse, and sometimes even bringing about death. The mark of violating the precepts is exactly the same — hence it is called violation.

items.en: Ten Kinds of Upholding, from Beginner to Buddhahood
items.zh: 持戒清淨 · 明持犯（二）
parent: VI. Distinguishing the Preliminary Expedient Means of Dhyāna-Pāramitā
分別禪波羅蜜前方便第六之一

zh: 第二、廣明持犯者，從初心至佛果，以明持犯有十種：一、持不缺戒，謂持初四重不犯。二、持不破戒，謂對僧殘不犯。三、持不穿戒，謂對下三篇不犯。四、持無瑕戒，亦名不雜戒，謂不起諂心及諸惱覺觀雜念，亦名定共戒。五、持隨道戒，即是心行十六行觀，發苦忍智慧，亦名道共戒。六、持無著戒，即阿那含人若斷欲界九品思惟盡，名斷律儀戒，乃至色愛、無色愛等諸結使盡，皆名無著戒。七、持智所讚戒，發菩提心，為令一切眾生得涅槃故持戒。如是持戒，則為智所讚歎，亦可言持菩薩十重四十八輕戒。此戒能至佛果，故為智所讚歎。八、持自在戒，菩薩持戒，於種種破戒緣中而得自在，亦可言菩薩知罪、不罪不可得故，但隨利益眾生而持戒，心無所執，故名自在戒。九、持具足戒，菩薩能具一切眾生戒法及上地戒。十、持隨定戒，不起滅定，現種種威儀戒法，以度眾生。
en: Second, extensively clarifying upholding and violation: from the first arising of the mind through to buddhahood, upholding the precepts is distinguished into ten kinds. First, upholding the precepts without deficiency — meaning upholding the initial four grave precepts without violating them. Second, upholding the precepts without breach — meaning not violating the saṅgha-remainder offenses. Third, upholding the precepts without perforation — meaning not violating the lower three categories of offense. Fourth, upholding the precepts without blemish, also called upholding them without mixture — meaning not giving rise to a flattering mind or to the scattered, vexing thoughts of coarse and subtle discursive thinking; also called the precepts held together with concentration. Fifth, upholding the precepts in accordance with the path — this is the mind's practice of the sixteen aspects of contemplation, bringing forth the wisdom of forbearance regarding suffering; also called the precepts held together with the path. Sixth, upholding the precepts without attachment — this refers to the non-returner who has completely severed the nine grades of discursive affliction of the desire realm, called severing the precepts of restraint, up through the exhaustion of every fetter such as craving for form and craving for the formless — all of these are called precepts without attachment. Seventh, upholding the precepts praised by wisdom — giving rise to the bodhi-mind, upholding the precepts so that all sentient beings may attain nirvāṇa. Precepts upheld in this way are praised by wisdom; this may also be spoken of as upholding the bodhisattva's ten major and forty-eight minor precepts. These precepts are able to lead all the way to buddhahood, and are therefore praised by wisdom. Eighth, upholding the precepts with mastery — the bodhisattva, upholding the precepts, attains mastery amid every kind of condition that might break them; this may also be spoken of as: since the bodhisattva knows that offense and non-offense cannot ultimately be found, they uphold the precepts solely in accordance with benefiting sentient beings, with a mind that grasps at nothing — hence this is called the precepts of mastery. Ninth, upholding the precepts in their completeness — the bodhisattva is able to be complete in the precept-dharmas of all sentient beings, together with the precepts proper to the higher grounds. Tenth, upholding the precepts in accordance with concentration — without rising from the concentration of cessation, manifesting every kind of dignified precept-conduct in order to bring sentient beings across.

zh: 前四即是世間戒淨，亦得出世間戒，義具如前說，善應分別；中二是出世間戒淨；後四是出世間上上戒淨。若能如上所說受持，是持戒相；異上所說，即是犯相。是名從初心至佛果，淺深論持戒及犯戒相。故經言：「唯佛一人具淨戒，餘人皆名破戒者。」復次，今明持戒者但隨分隨力而修習，令增進漸漸清淨；若不爾者，不能生諸禪定。復次，頓行菩薩能以慧方便，從初發心一念之中即具持十種戒，是故經言：「發心畢竟二不別。」
en: The first four of these are the purity of the precepts belonging to the worldly, though they may also give rise to world-transcending precepts — this meaning is complete as already explained above, and should be carefully distinguished. The middle two are the purity of the world-transcending precepts. The last four are the purity of the precepts transcending the world and beyond. If one is able to receive and uphold the precepts as described above, this is the mark of upholding; whatever differs from what is described above is the mark of violation. This is what is meant by discussing the shallow and the deep marks of upholding and violating the precepts, from the first arising of the mind all the way to buddhahood. Hence the sūtra says: "Only the Buddha alone is complete in pure precepts; everyone else is called one who has broken the precepts."

Furthermore, here it is clarified that upholding the precepts is cultivated only according to one's own portion and one's own power, allowing for gradual advancement toward purity; if this were not so, one would be unable to give rise to any dhyāna-concentration whatsoever. Furthermore, the bodhisattva of sudden practice, by means of wisdom and skillful means, is able, within a single thought-moment at the very first arising of the mind, to already be complete in upholding all ten kinds of precepts — hence the sūtra says: "The arising of the mind and its ultimate completion are, in the end, not two different things."

This ten-stage ladder is the treatise's own answer to a question implicit in "the presence or absence of precepts": having precepts at all is binary, but upholding them well is a matter of degree, spanning the entire path. The first three stages sort ordinary monastic offenses by severity (the four grave offenses, the saṅgha-remainder offenses, and the lower three categories), and the fourth is the precept held together with concentration; the middle two belong to path attainment; the last four are the bodhisattva's own, culminating in a precept-holding so free of self-grasping that "offense and non-offense cannot ultimately be found." The closing citation — "the arising of the mind and its ultimate completion are, in the end, not two different things" — is the same "identity of beginning and end" move already seen at the close of fascicle 1's topic 2.

items.zh: 持戒清淨 · 明持犯（三）· 明覆發
parent: VI. Distinguishing the Preliminary Expedient Means of Dhyāna-Pāramitā
分別禪波羅蜜前方便第六之一

zh: 第三、明覆發。就中自有二意：一者、正明覆發；二者、簡定。云何名覆發相？行者持戒，能發禪定破戒，即覆禪定。行者持世間戒淨故，即發世間禪；若持世間戒不淨，即覆世間禪。出世間戒及出世間上上戒，持則發禪，毀則覆禪，類如是分別。
en: Third, clarifying concealment and manifestation. This too has two parts in itself: first, directly clarifying concealment and manifestation; second, settling points of doubt. What is called the mark of concealment and manifestation? When a practitioner upholds the precepts, dhyāna-concentration can be brought forth; when the precepts are broken, dhyāna-concentration is concealed. Because the practitioner upholds the purity of the worldly precepts, worldly dhyāna is brought forth; if the worldly precepts are held impurely, worldly dhyāna is concealed. The same distinction applies, by the same kind of reasoning, to the world-transcending precepts and the precepts transcending the world and beyond: upheld, dhyāna is brought forth; violated, dhyāna is concealed.

zh: 二者、簡定覆發者，為眾生現在修禪不定故，應作四句分別：一、自有雖犯戒而發定，持而不發；二、自有破戒而不發定，持戒而發；三、自有持戒、犯戒二俱發；四、自有持、犯俱不發。初一、犯戒之人修禪定而發者，是過去習因，善根深厚，今雖有罪，過去善根力強故，亦以現前修禪定，重慚愧為緣故，譬如負債，強者先牽，所以得有發定之義。二、次持戒而不發定者，是人過去不種深禪定之因，今生雖復持戒修定，而不即發。三、俱發，四、俱不發，悉可類釋，故有四種不同。尋其根源，要因持戒而發，犯戒終為遮障。何以故？若過去經得禪定，即知過去以曾持戒發定故，成今世之習因；今生復以慚愧懺悔清淨為緣，是故得發宿世善根也。
en: Second, as to settling points of doubt about concealment and manifestation: because sentient beings, cultivating dhyāna in the present, are not uniform in this regard, the matter should be sorted into a fourfold classification: first, there are those who, though violating the precepts, still give rise to concentration, while others who uphold them do not give rise to it; second, there are those who break the precepts and do not give rise to concentration, while others who uphold the precepts do give rise to it; third, there are those in whom both upholding the precepts and violating them alike give rise to concentration; fourth, there are those in whom neither upholding nor violating gives rise to it.

As to the first — a person who violates the precepts yet gives rise to concentration through cultivating dhyāna — this is because of a habituated cause from a past life: the wholesome roots are deep and strong, and though there is an offense in the present, the power of the past wholesome roots is strong; and further, because present cultivation of dhyāna together with deep shame and remorse serve as conditions — it is like a debt, where the stronger creditor is paid first — this is how the meaning of "giving rise to concentration" comes about in such a case. Second, as to one who upholds the precepts yet does not give rise to concentration: such a person did not, in the past, plant the cause of deep dhyāna-concentration, and so, though upholding the precepts and cultivating concentration in this present life, it is not immediately brought forth. Third, both giving rise to it, and fourth, neither giving rise to it, may both be explained by the same kind of reasoning — hence these four distinct kinds. Tracing this to its root, it is essentially through upholding the precepts that concentration is brought forth, while violating the precepts is, in the end, an obstruction to it. Why is this? If dhyāna-concentration was attained in a past life, then it is known that, in the past, concentration was brought forth precisely through upholding the precepts, becoming the habituated cause of the present life; and in this present life, shame, remorse, repentance, and purity again serve as the condition through which the wholesome roots of past lives are brought forth once more.

This fourfold classification is a piece of pastoral realism embedded in a technical treatise: Zhiyi has just spent several paragraphs establishing that upholding precepts is what properly gives rise to dhyāna — and then immediately acknowledges the obvious counter-cases, someone who breaks precepts yet still experiences concentration, or upholds them scrupulously yet experiences nothing. The explanation reaches back into past-life causation rather than abandoning the general rule: current dhyāna experience is read as the ripening of past habituated causes, with present moral conduct (and repentance where needed) serving as the condition that allows those causes to bear fruit now. This closes 持犯 (upholding and violation), the second of condition 1's three parts.

items.en: Setting the Mind of Repentance in Motion

zh: 第三、明懺悔中，自有二意：一者、先明運懺悔心；二者、正明懺悔方法。第一、云何名運懺悔之心？若人性自不作惡，則無罪可悔。行人既不能決定持戒，或於中間值遇惡緣，即便破毀，若輕若重，以戒破故，則尸羅不淨，三昧不生，譬如衣有垢膩，不受染色，是故宜須懺悔。以懺悔故，則戒品清淨，三昧可生，如衣垢污，若浣清潔，染之可著。行者如是思惟，若戒不清淨，決須懺悔。
en: Third, clarifying repentance: this too has two parts in itself — first, clarifying how to set the mind of repentance in motion; second, rightly clarifying the method of repentance.

First, what is meant by setting the mind of repentance in motion? If a person's own nature simply never commits any evil, there is no offense to repent of. But since a practitioner is not always able to uphold the precepts with unwavering resolve, and may, at some point, encounter an unwholesome condition and thereby break them — whether gravely or lightly — once the precepts are broken, moral discipline is no longer pure, and samādhi cannot arise, just as cloth stained with grime will not properly take a dye. This is why repentance is necessary. Through repentance, the precepts become pure once more and samādhi can arise — just as cloth stained with grime, once washed clean, can properly take a dye. Reflecting in this way, the practitioner comes to know: if the precepts are not pure, repentance is absolutely necessary.

zh: 是故經云：「佛法之中有二種健兒：一、性不作惡；二、作已能悔。」今造過知悔，名健人也。夫懺悔者，懺名懺謝三寶及一切眾生，悔名慚愧，改過求哀。我今此罪，若得滅者，於將來時，寧失身命，終不更造如斯苦業。如比丘白佛：「我寧抱是熾然大火，終不敢毀犯如來淨戒。」生如是心，唯願三寶證明攝受，是名懺悔。復次，懺名外不覆藏，悔則內心剋責；懺名知罪為惡，悔則恐受其報。如是眾多，今不廣說，舉要言之，若能知法虛妄，永息惡業，修行善道，是名懺悔。
en: Hence the sūtra says: "Within the Buddhadharma there are two kinds of courageous person: first, one whose nature simply never commits evil; second, one who, having done wrong, is able to repent of it." To commit a transgression and yet know to repent of it is what makes one such a courageous person.

As for what repentance itself is: "confession" means confessing before, and begging forgiveness of, the Three Jewels and all sentient beings; "repentance" means a sense of shame and remorse, correcting one's faults and beseeching compassion. One reflects: "If this offense of mine can now be extinguished, then in time to come, though I should lose my very body and life, I will never again commit such a painful karmic deed." As a monk once said to the Buddha: "I would rather embrace a raging, blazing fire than dare to violate and break the Tathāgata's pure precepts." Giving rise to a mind such as this, wishing only that the Three Jewels bear witness and receive one in compassion — this is called repentance. Furthermore: "confession" means not concealing one's fault outwardly, while "repentance" means holding oneself strictly to account inwardly; "confession" means knowing that the offense was evil, while "repentance" means fearing to receive its retribution. There is much more that could be said of this kind, which will not be given in full here — taking the essential point: if one is able to know that dharmas are illusory and unreal, forever setting unwholesome karma to rest and cultivating the wholesome path, this is what is called repentance.

quiz.q: Clarifying upholding and violation has three parts. Which are they?
options: upholding in body, speech, mind
five categories, seven groups, ten benefits
briefly, extensively through each stage, and concealment and manifestation
upholding, violation, repentance
quiz.why: "Clarifying upholding and violation: this has three parts in itself — first, briefly clarifying upholding and violation; second, extensively clarifying upholding and violation through each successive stage; third, clarifying concealment and manifestation." Repentance is the third part of pure discipline, not of this section.

quiz.q: Which of the following is among the ten benefits of upholding precepts quoted from the Vinaya?
options: attaining the five powers
rebirth in heaven
bringing faith to those without it; increasing the faith of those who have it
gaining great wealth
quiz.why: The ten include gathering the saṅgha, subduing the arrogant, "so as to bring faith to those without it; seventh, so as to increase the faith of those who already have it," checking present contaminants, and helping those of pure conduct long abide. Powers, heaven, and wealth are not among them.

quiz.q: Which two similes does the text use for guarding and upholding the precepts?
options: like a potter kneading clay; like tuning a lute
like a debt paid to the strongest creditor; like drilling for fire
like grimy cloth; like soap-pod lye
like guarding an inflated float, not discarding the smallest part; like carrying a bowl brimful of oil
quiz.why: "Like guarding an inflated float used to cross water, not discarding it even to the smallest degree — hence this is called guarding and maintaining, also called firmly upholding, as in the simile of carrying a bowl brimful of oil." Grimy cloth and lye belong to repentance, the debt to concealment and manifestation, and the potter and lute to harmonizing the five things.

quiz.q: The text gives two meanings of "violation." What are they?
options: bodily and mental violation
grave and minor offenses
deliberate and accidental violation
going against: turning back midway; coming into contact with what harms: like breaking a medicine's dietary rule and undermining it
quiz.why: "'Violation' means going against and transgressing ... one turns back midway, whether in a grave or a lesser matter." "Furthermore, 'violation' also means coming into contact with what harms. It is like someone taking medicine who has been instructed to abstain from certain foods." Grave and minor are degrees within the first sense, not the two meanings.

quiz.q: According to the text, for what reason do the seven kinds of persons guard their precepts without violation?
options: for fame
out of fear of expulsion
for the sake of the ten benefits
to be born in heaven
quiz.why: "The seven kinds of persons who receive the Buddha's restraining precepts guard and maintain them without violation for the sake of ten benefits." The ten benefits are those listed from the Vinaya.

quiz.q: In the first three of the ten kinds of upholding — without deficiency, without breach, without perforation — what does each refer to?
options: all three are the four grave precepts
all three are bodhisattva precepts
without deficiency: the four grave precepts; without breach: saṅgha-remainder offenses; without perforation: the lower three categories
the reverse order
quiz.why: "First, upholding the precepts without deficiency — meaning upholding the initial four grave precepts without violating them. Second, upholding the precepts without breach — meaning not violating the saṅgha-remainder offenses. Third, upholding the precepts without perforation — meaning not violating the lower three categories of offense."

quiz.q: What are "precepts without blemish" and "precepts in accordance with the path" also called?
options: the reverse
without blemish: precepts held together with concentration; in accordance with the path: precepts held together with the path
both are the precepts of restraint by severance
both are precepts of mastery
quiz.why: "Fourth, upholding the precepts without blemish, also called upholding them without mixture ... also called the precepts held together with concentration. Fifth, upholding the precepts in accordance with the path ... also called the precepts held together with the path." Severance-restraint appears under the sixth.

options: only the Buddha
the non-returner who has severed the nine grades of desire-realm affliction, on up to the exhaustion of craving for form and the formless
one who holds the bodhisattva's ten major and forty-eight minor precepts
an ordinary beginner
quiz.why: "Sixth, upholding the precepts without attachment — this refers to the non-returner who has completely severed the nine grades of discursive affliction of the desire realm ... up through the exhaustion of every fetter such as craving for form and craving for the formless." The bodhisattva precepts belong to the seventh kind.

quiz.q: Why is the eighth kind called "upholding the precepts with mastery"?
options: because one never rises from cessation
knowing offense and non-offense cannot be found, the bodhisattva upholds the precepts only for beings' benefit, grasping at nothing
because one may freely ignore the precepts
because one has gained powers
quiz.why: "Since the bodhisattva knows that offense and non-offense cannot ultimately be found, they uphold the precepts solely in accordance with benefiting sentient beings, with a mind that grasps at nothing — hence this is called the precepts of mastery." Mastery is not ignoring the precepts; not rising from cessation is the tenth kind.

quiz.q: How are the ten kinds of upholding matched to worldly, world-transcending, and beyond?
options: the first four worldly; the middle two world-transcending; the last four beyond the world
five and five
three, four, three
all ten world-transcending
quiz.why: "The first four of these are the purity of the precepts belonging to the worldly ... The middle two are the purity of the world-transcending precepts. The last four are the purity of the precepts transcending the world and beyond." The middle two are the path-accordant and non-attached precepts.

quiz.q: After quoting "Only the Buddha alone is complete in pure precepts; everyone else is called one who has broken the precepts," what does the text say for practitioners?
options: since all have broken them, no need to keep them
uphold according to one's portion and power, advancing gradually toward purity; otherwise no dhyāna can arise
one must first become a buddha to meditate
only those holding all ten may meditate
quiz.why: "Here it is clarified that upholding the precepts is cultivated only according to one's own portion and one's own power, allowing for gradual advancement toward purity; if this were not so, one would be unable to give rise to any dhyāna-concentration whatsoever."

quiz.q: How does the bodhisattva of sudden practice uphold the ten kinds of precepts?
options: only the first four
by wisdom and skillful means, complete in all ten within a single thought at the first arising of the mind
one by one in sequence
sudden-practice bodhisattvas keep no precepts
quiz.why: "The bodhisattva of sudden practice, by means of wisdom and skillful means, is able, within a single thought-moment at the very first arising of the mind, to already be complete in upholding all ten kinds of precepts."

options: emerging from and entering concentration
hiding and confessing offenses
upholding the precepts brings dhyāna forth; breaking them conceals it
covering the hindrances and raising the faculties
quiz.why: "When a practitioner upholds the precepts, dhyāna-concentration can be brought forth; when the precepts are broken, dhyāna-concentration is concealed." It concerns precepts and dhyāna, not hiding or confessing offenses.

quiz.q: How does the text explain someone who breaks precepts yet gives rise to concentration, and what simile does it use?
options: because breaking precepts does not affect dhyāna
it is a demonic state
like mending torn cloth
deep wholesome roots from past habituation, plus present cultivation and remorse as conditions — like a debt where the stronger creditor is paid first
quiz.why: "This is because of a habituated cause from a past life: the wholesome roots are deep and strong ... and further, because present cultivation of dhyāna together with deep shame and remorse serve as conditions — it is like a debt, where the stronger creditor is paid first." The conclusion still holds that concentration arises through upholding the precepts.

quiz.q: Tracing the fourfold classification to its root, what does the text conclude?
options: only this life matters, not the past
those who break precepts attain concentration more easily
concentration essentially arises through upholding the precepts, while violation is in the end an obstruction
precepts and concentration are unrelated
quiz.why: "Tracing this to its root, it is essentially through upholding the precepts that concentration is brought forth, while violating the precepts is, in the end, an obstruction to it." Even the exception is explained by past precept-holding becoming a present habituated cause.

quiz.q: Why, according to the text, is repentance necessary once the precepts are broken, and what simile is used?
options: without repentance one is expelled from the saṅgha
like a potter kneading clay
like guarding a float, not discarding the smallest part
impure discipline keeps samādhi from arising, like grimy cloth that will not take dye; washed clean, it can be dyed
quiz.why: "Once the precepts are broken, moral discipline is no longer pure, and samādhi cannot arise, just as cloth stained with grime will not properly take a dye. This is why repentance is necessary." Guarding the float illustrates upholding, and the potter illustrates harmonizing the five things.

quiz.q: The sūtra says there are two kinds of courageous person in the Buddhadharma. Which?
options: one whose nature never commits evil; one who, having done wrong, can repent
monastics and lay people
one who keeps precepts; one who cultivates concentration
the learned and the ascetic
quiz.why: "Within the Buddhadharma there are two kinds of courageous person: first, one whose nature simply never commits evil; second, one who, having done wrong, is able to repent of it."

quiz.q: In the second pair of definitions, how does the text distinguish 懺 and 悔?
options: 懺 before the Buddha, 悔 before the saṅgha
懺: not concealing outwardly, 悔: holding oneself to account inwardly; 懺: knowing the offense was evil, 悔: fearing its retribution
the two mean exactly the same
懺 is speech, 悔 is prostration
quiz.why: "Furthermore: 'confession' means not concealing one's fault outwardly, while 'repentance' means holding oneself strictly to account inwardly; 'confession' means knowing that the offense was evil, while 'repentance' means fearing to receive its retribution."

quiz.q: Taking the essential point, what does the text say repentance is?
options: simply telling one's teacher all faults
reciting a repentance text daily
making offerings to offset offenses
knowing dharmas to be illusory, forever setting unwholesome karma to rest, and cultivating the wholesome path
quiz.why: "Taking the essential point: if one is able to know that dharmas are illusory and unreal, forever setting unwholesome karma to rest and cultivating the wholesome path, this is what is called repentance."
